newsitem.title: INDIA: India urges farmers to sell wheat to state firms.
newsitem.headline: India urges farmers to sell wheat to state firms.

text.p: Indian Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra on Wednesday appealed to wheat farmers to sell their produce to state-run agencies to help government's wheat buying operations.
Farmers in agriculturally-rich northern Indian states have clashed with the government over wheat purchase prices, threatening procurement operations as stocks diminish.

Government ministers earlier this month agreed to pay a bonus of 600 rupees ($16.80) per tonne to farmers in addition to the current purchase price of 4,150 rupees. But farmers said this was below their expectations.
The bonus will be payable on wheat offered for sale to procurement agencies for the central pool up to June 10, 1997.
Farmers in the states of Punjab and Haryana, which contribute about 80 percent of the country's wheat output, have been demanding prices equal to the levels at which the government imports wheat.
An Agriculture Ministry statement quoted Mishra as saying he had recieved reports that farmers were planning to start agitating against selling their produce to government agencies.
"This will not be beneficial to farmers," the statement said.
"Even if farmers believe that they were not getting the correct price for their produce, they can come and present their problems," the statement quoted Mishra as saying.
News reports quoted Punjab farmers as saying that they would not sell any wheat to the state agencies from Wednesday in a bid to extract higher prices from the government.
The government buys wheat to build up its buffer stocks, which it then uses to control prices by releasing stocks through a state-run distribution system.

Officials said the state-run grain procurement agency the Food Corporation of India (FCI) had bought only 260,000 tonnes of wheat so far compared with 1.4 million tonnes at the same time last year. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
